name: The twenty-five principles (pañcaviṃśati-tattva)

definitions.definition: Reality enumerated as twenty-five principles: puruṣa; mūlaprakṛti, which is not a product; seven principles that are both products and producers — mahat (buddhi), ahaṃkāra and the five subtle elements; and sixteen that are products only — manas, the five sense capacities, the five action capacities and the five gross elements (SK 3, 22; SS 1.61; Tattvasamāsa 1–3). 'The knower of the twenty-five principles is liberated in any stage of life' (verse quoted by Gauḍapāda and the Jayamaṅgalā).

members: 5–9 the five tanmātras (sound, touch, form, taste, smell) — producers and products
11–15 the five buddhīndriyas (ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose) — products only
16–20 the five karmendriyas (speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals) — products only
21–25 the five mahābhūtas (space, air, fire, water, earth) — products only

relations.note: Śaiva schemes of thirty-six principles include these twenty-five as their lower principles (the Śaiva account; interpretive link)

name: Order of emergence and re-absorption (sañcara, pratisañcara)

definitions.definition: From prakṛti arises mahat; from mahat ahaṃkāra; from ahaṃkāra the group of sixteen — the eleven organs from its sāttvika (vaikṛta) aspect and the five subtle elements from its tāmasa (bhūtādi) aspect, both with its taijasa aspect; from the five subtle elements the five gross elements (SK 22, 24–25; SS 1.61) — sound→space, touch→air, form→fire, taste→water, smell→earth (Gauḍapāda). In re-absorption each dissolves into its cause in reverse order; the unmanifest does not dissolve (Tattvasamāsa commentaries). The Yuktidīpikā records divergent orders taught by Vindhyavāsin and others.

Sattva, rajas and tamas, the constituents of prakṛti and all its products: of the nature of pleasure, pain and delusion; illuminating, activating and restraining; light, mobile and heavy; they dominate, support and produce one another and work together for one purpose like the parts of a lamp (SK 12–13). Prakṛti is their equilibrium (SS 1.61); creation abounds in sattva above, rajas in the middle and tamas below (SK 54).

The effect exists in its material cause before production: the non-existent cannot be produced; a definite material is taken up; not everything comes from everything; the capable produces what it can; the effect has the nature of its cause (SK 9; SS 1.114–118). Production is manifestation, destruction is dissolution into the cause (SS 1.121). It grounds the inference of prakṛti from its effects (SK 14–16).

relations.note: Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika's new-effect view, rejected in SK 9
the pre-existent effect points to an unmanifest cause

definitions.definition: Prakṛti really transforms into its products through the guṇas, by combination and transformation, like water differing in different receptacles (SK 16); the world so produced is real (SS 6.52).

Being struck by the three sufferings prompts the inquiry (SK 1); the commentators name them internal (bodily and mental), from other beings, and from the divine (Gauḍapāda, Vācaspati). Seen and Vedic remedies do not end them certainly and finally (SK 1–2); their complete cessation is the supreme goal (SS 1.1). Suffering from old age and death belongs to embodied existence until the subtle body ceases (SK 55); the discriminating count even pleasure as suffering (SS 6.6–8).

The discriminating knowledge of the manifest, the unmanifest and the knower (SK 2), accomplished by buddhi (SK 37) and culminating, through repeated practice of the principles, in the complete, pure and single knowledge 'I am not, not mine, not I' (SK 64); it is the direct realization of the distinctness of sattva and puruṣa (Vācaspati). Liberation comes from it alone (SS 3.23–25); it is reached by renouncing each principle with 'not this, not this' (SS 3.76).

The conscious principle, neither producer nor product (SK 3), the opposite of the guṇa-made (SK 11): witness, isolated, neutral, seer, non-agent (SK 19), unattached and by nature ever free (SS 1.15–19), light itself, without consciousness as a property (SS 1.145–146). Its existence is proved because aggregates are for another, because something must stand opposite the guṇas, because of control, experience and the striving for isolation (SK 17). It is many (SK 18). It is not truly bound or released (SK 62).

relations.note: Both name the self; Sāṃkhya insists on plurality and non-agency, which Advaita's one ātman and Nyāya's qualified ātman do not share (graded partial; interpretive)

definitions.definition: Puruṣas are many, because birth, death and instruments are allotted separately, beings do not act all at once, and the guṇas are differently proportioned (SK 18; SS 1.149, 6.45); some were liberated while others were not (SS 1.157). Scriptures of non-duality refer to sameness of kind, not number (SS 1.154).

The unconscious, productive root (mūlaprakṛti, pradhāna, the unmanifest): uncaused, one, common, of three guṇas in equilibrium (SK 3, 10–11; SS 1.61). Not perceived because subtle, it is inferred from its effects (SK 8): from the limited measure of things, their homogeneity, activity through potency, the distinction of cause and effect and the merging of the manifold (SK 15–16). It acts for puruṣa like milk for the calf (SK 57), withdraws like a dancer once seen (SK 59), and is what is truly bound and released (SK 62). Gauḍapāda lists its synonyms pradhāna, brahman, avyakta, bahudhānaka, māyā; there is only one prakṛti (Gauḍapāda on SK 66).

relations.note: Advaita's māyā is not a second reality (the Sāṃkhya–Advaita contrast; interpretive)

definitions.definition: The manifest is caused, impermanent, non-pervasive, active, many, dependent, merging, composite and subordinate; the unmanifest is the opposite (SK 10); both consist of the three guṇas and are non-discriminating, objects, common, unconscious and productive, unlike puruṣa (SK 11).

The subtle body, produced first, unattached, constant, made of the principles from mahat down to the subtle elements (buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas, the ten capacities and the five subtle elements), transmigrates, perfumed by the dispositions, without enjoying (SK 40); it needs a support like a picture or shadow (SK 41) and plays its parts like an actor (SK 42). The subtle bodies are constant; the bodies born of mother and father perish (SK 39). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra calls it 'seventeen, one' (3.9) and admits a conveying (ātivāhika) body (5.103). Vindhyavāsin denied the subtle body (Yuktidīpikā on SK 39).

relations.note: corresponds to the subtle body of Vedānta's three bodies, though composed differently (interpretive)

definitions.definition: Buddhi's sāttvika form is virtue, knowledge, dispassion and power; its tāmasa form their opposites (SK 23). They are innate, natural or acquired (SK 43); they perfume the subtle body (SK 40). Virtue leads upward, non-virtue downward, knowledge to liberation, error to bondage; dispassion to absorption in prakṛti, passion to saṃsāra, power to non-obstruction (SK 44–45). By seven of them prakṛti binds herself, by one (knowledge) she releases herself (SK 63).

name: The creation of cognitions (pratyaya-sarga): the fifty

definitions.definition: The intellectual creation of fifty kinds: five errors (darkness, delusion, great delusion, gloom, blind gloom; 62 subdivisions), twenty-eight incapacities (11 injuries of the organs, 17 of buddhi), nine contentments and eight accomplishments (SK 46–51). Error, incapacity and contentment curb accomplishment (SK 51). With the ten fundamental topics they make the sixty topics of the Ṣaṣṭitantra.

The goal: when discrimination arises, prakṛti — her purpose served — ceases for that puruṣa like a dancer who has shown herself (SK 59, 65–66); the knower remains embodied for a time (SK 67), and at the body's end attains isolation that is certain and final (SK 68). It is not the manifestation of bliss, nor going anywhere, nor annihilation (SS 5.74–83), but the destruction of obstacles (SS 6.20) and the complete cessation of the threefold suffering (SS 1.1, 3.85). Strictly, bondage and release belong to prakṛti (SK 62).

Dispassion leads to absorption into prakṛti (SK 45) — not liberation: those who take prakṛti or its evolutes for the self dissolve into them (Gauḍapāda on SK 48, 'darkness') and rise again like a diver (SS 3.54); the Kramadīpikā calls it 'bondage to prakṛti'. The one who rises may become an all-knowing lord in the next creation (SS 3.55–57).

After perfect knowledge, virtue and the rest cease to cause, but the knower remains embodied through the momentum of impressions, like a potter's wheel (SK 67); knowledge burns future karma like burnt seeds (Gauḍapāda). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra names the one liberated while living and grounds it in the need for liberated teachers — otherwise the blind would lead the blind (3.78–84).

Sāṃkhya's final isolation: 'when separation from the body is attained and pradhāna ceases, its purpose fulfilled, he attains isolation both certain and final' (SK 68). The SK does not use the word videhamukti.

Sāṃkhya accepts three: perception (determination concerning each object), inference (threefold; from general correlation for things beyond the senses) and reliable testimony (for what neither establishes) (SK 4–6); other proposed means are included in these (SK 4; Vācaspati). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra defines perception as cognition that, in contact, reflects its object (1.89).

Existing things go unperceived through excessive distance, excessive nearness, impaired senses, inattention, subtlety, obstruction, being overpowered and mixture with the similar (SK 7); prakṛti is unperceived through subtlety (SK 8).

The instrument is thirteenfold — buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas (internal) and the ten capacities (external); it seizes, holds and illuminates (SK 32–33). The internal works in three times, the external in the present; the internal is the door-keeper, the external the doors (SK 33, 35). The organs act by one another's impulse, for puruṣa's purpose alone (SK 31), and like lamps present that purpose to buddhi (SK 36).
In Sāṃkhya threefold: buddhi, ahaṃkāra and manas, each with its own function, sharing the five vital winds as their common function (SK 29, 33).

Prāṇa and the others are the shared function of the three internal instruments (SK 29; SS 2.31); the Kramadīpikā places prāṇa at mouth and nose, apāna at the navel, samāna at the heart, udāna at the throat, vyāna at the joints.

The first evolute (= mahat), whose nature is determination; bearer of the eight dispositions (SK 23); it accomplishes all experience for puruṣa and discriminates puruṣa from pradhāna (SK 37); unconscious, it appears conscious by taking on the shade of consciousness (Vācaspati on SK 5).
The principle of self-assertion (SK 24), from which the organs and subtle elements proceed in its vaikṛta, bhūtādi and taijasa aspects (SK 25); it, not puruṣa, is the agent (SS 6.54).
The eleventh organ, partaking of both sense and action capacities, whose function is construction (saṅkalpa) (SK 27).
The non-specific elements of sound, touch, form, taste and smell, from ahaṃkāra as bhūtādi, from which the gross elements arise (SK 22, 25, 38).
Space, air, fire, water and earth, arising from the five subtle elements; specific, and calm, turbulent or dull (SK 22, 38).
Five sense capacities (ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose), five action capacities (speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals) and manas, all from ahaṃkāra (SK 24–28); not made of the elements (SS 2.20, 5.84).

name: The two purposes: experience and release

definitions.definition: Prakṛti acts for puruṣa's sake — for another as if for itself (SK 56, 60) — for experience and release; the conjunction is for seeing and for isolation (SK 21); like milk flowing for the calf (SK 57) or people acting to satisfy a longing (SK 58); once both purposes are fulfilled there is no motive for creation (SK 66; Gauḍapāda).

name: The conjunction of puruṣa and prakṛti (saṃyoga)

definitions.definition: Their conjunction, like that of the lame and the blind, produces creation (SK 21), makes the unconscious seem conscious and the indifferent seem an agent (SK 20); it is due to non-discrimination (SS 1.55) and its cause is variously given as karma, non-discrimination (Pañcaśikha) or the subtle body (Sanandana) (SS 6.67–69).

Classical Sāṃkhya posits no established Īśvara: the SK does not mention one; Gauḍapāda argues that the attributeless Īśvara could not produce what has guṇas (on SK 61); the Sāṃkhya Sūtra holds that Īśvara is not established (1.92–99), that karma, not a Lord, yields fruit (5.2–12), and that effects depend on ahaṃkāra, not Īśvara (6.64) — yet it admits emergent lords: the one absorbed in prakṛti who becomes all-knowing and all-doing (3.55–57). Vijñānabhikṣu salutes the Lord (Sāṃkhyasāra 1.1.1).

name: Theistic Sāṃkhya (seśvara)

definitions.definition: Forms of Sāṃkhya that admit a Lord: the epic 'twenty-sixth principle' above the twenty-five (Mahābhārata, Mokṣadharma), Purāṇic accounts where emergence from pradhāna proceeds under the Lord and Kapila is an avatāra (Māṭhara on SK 1; Bhāgavata Purāṇa), a Pāñcarātra Ṣaṣṭitantra (Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā), Yoga as 'Sāṃkhya with Īśvara' in doxographies, and Vijñānabhikṣu, who salutes mahat as the self-born Lord and treats the Sāṃkhya Sūtra's denial of Īśvara as concessive.

notes: Mahābhārata and Ahirbudhnya chapter details recalled, not checked.

name: Early (pre-classical) Sāṃkhya

definitions.definition: The tradition traces Sāṃkhya to Kapila, Āsuri and Pañcaśikha and to teachers such as Janaka, Vasiṣṭha and Dvaipāyana (Yuktidīpikā on SK 72). Earlier formulations are preserved in the Mahābhārata's Mokṣadharma (Pañcaśikha's teaching to Janaka; Vasiṣṭha–Karāla and Yājñavalkya–Janaka dialogues with 24/25/26 principles), in the Bhagavad Gītā's 'sāṃkhya' (knowledge) and field-knower teaching (ch. 13–14, 18.13), in Caraka's account of twenty-four principles (Śārīrasthāna 1), and in Aśvaghoṣa's report of Arāḍa's teaching (Buddhacarita 12, a Buddhist report). Upaniṣadic hierarchies (Kaṭha 3.10–11) and the word 'sāṃkhya' (Śvetāśvatara 6.13) are claimed by Sāṃkhya as its scriptural basis.

relations.note: early enumerations precede the classical 25 (scholarly view)

notes: Refers to U05 (Mahābhārata, Gītā), U30 (Caraka), U03 (Upaniṣads); chapter refs recalled, not checked.

name: The sixty topics of the Ṣaṣṭitantra

definitions.definition: The SK's topics are those of the whole Ṣaṣṭitantra without its tales and polemics (SK 72). The sixty are ten fundamental topics — pradhāna's existence, oneness, purposiveness; puruṣa's distinctness; being for another; plurality of puruṣas; separation; conjunction; the remaining function; non-agency — and the fifty of the creation of cognitions (Yuktidīpikā introductory verses; Māṭhara on SK 72; Kramadīpikā; Vācaspati quoting the Rājavārttika).

Kapila, the supreme sage and first knower, gave the teaching out of compassion to Āsuri, Āsuri to Pañcaśikha, who expanded it; through a succession of pupils it reached Īśvarakṛṣṇa (SK 69–71). The Māṭhara Vṛtti names Bhārgava, Ulūka, Vālmīki, Hārīta and Devala; the Yuktidīpikā names Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya and Mūka, adding that the full lineage cannot be told because it began with the Blessed One. Gauḍapāda places Kapila among Brahmā's seven sons with Āsuri, Voḍhu and Pañcaśikha.

name: Teacher, student and transmission in Sāṃkhya

definitions.definition: The teaching is secret (SK 69), given out of compassion (SK 70), to a qualified student: Kapila tested Āsuri three times over thousand-year intervals before he renounced (Māṭhara). Acquired knowledge arises with the teacher as its occasioning cause (Gauḍapāda on SK 43); among the accomplishments are hearing, study, approaching a teacher and serving the venerable (Gauḍapāda on SK 51). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra: instruction must be repeated (4.3); take the essence from many teachers like a bee (4.13); hearing without reflection does not suffice, as with Virocana, while Indra attained after obeisance, continence and long approach (4.17–19); a defiled mind lets the seed of instruction fail (4.29–30); there must be liberated teachers, else the blind lead the blind (3.80–82); there is no fixed rule since students differ (3.77).

Buddhi, unconscious, takes on the shade of consciousness and appears conscious, while puruṣa, reflected in it, appears to know and enjoy (Vācaspati on SK 5; cf. SK 20); the Sāṃkhya Sūtra speaks of coloring (uparāga) that is misidentification rather than real coloring, like the red flower and the crystal (1.164, 6.28). Vijñānabhikṣu is reported to teach a mutual reflection of puruṣa and buddhi (recalled, low confidence).

Puruṣa is witness, seer and neutral (SK 19), witness through direct relation (SS 1.161) and of deep sleep and other states (SS 1.148); upon knowledge it sees prakṛti like a spectator, at ease (SK 65).

name: The creation of beings and the worlds by guṇa

definitions.definition: Creation of beings is fourteenfold: eight divine, five animal, one human (SK 53); the upper worlds abound in sattva, the root in tamas, the middle in rajas, from Brahmā to a blade of grass (SK 54); even there suffering from old age and death is common (SK 55; SS 3.53). The Kramadīpikā names the eight divine classes (daiva, paiśāca, rākṣasa, yākṣa, gāndharva, aindra, prājāpatya, brāhma) and five animal (domestic animals, birds, wild beasts, reptiles, plants).

Reasoning, hearing, study, the three destructions of suffering, gaining friends and giving are the eight accomplishments conducive to knowledge (SK 51) — not supernormal powers (those are aiśvarya). Gauḍapāda explains each as a route to knowledge of the principles (reflection, hearing, study, approaching a teacher, a knowing friend, serving the venerable); Vācaspati is recalled as making the three destructions primary and the other five their means in sequence (low confidence).

Power is a sāttvika disposition of buddhi (SK 23) giving non-obstruction (SK 45); the commentators list becoming minute, great, light, reaching, irresistible will, lordship, control and going where one wishes (Gauḍapāda on SK 23). Warnings: attachment to the powers is the error 'delusion', through which gods like Indra fall back (Gauḍapāda on SK 48); gaining the powers is not liberation, since they end (SS 5.82; 4.32). Yogic powers are nonetheless not to be denied (SS 5.128).

In Sāṃkhya virtue and non-virtue are dispositions of buddhi, not of puruṣa (SK 23; SS 5.25); they carry the subtle body upward or downward (SK 44) and ripen as experience; the fruit of action comes from karma, not from a governing Lord (SS 5.2); with knowledge they cease to act as causes — future karma burnt like seeds, present karma exhausted (SK 67; Gauḍapāda).

At death the body born of mother and father perishes, while the constant subtle body, perfumed by the dispositions, transmigrates to divine, animal or human birth according to virtue and non-virtue (SK 39–40, 44, 53); suffering from old age and death lasts until the subtle body ceases (SK 55). The knower's body falls when impressions are exhausted, and isolation follows (SK 67–68). The teachers disagreed on the subtle body at death and birth (Yuktidīpikā on SK 39).

name: Sound, word and Veda in Sāṃkhya

definitions.definition: Sound is the subtle element from which space arises (SK 22 with Gauḍapāda); speech has sound as its object (SK 34). Testimony is one of three means of knowledge (SK 4–6). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra holds that the Vedas are neither eternal nor authored by a person, yet valid by their own manifest power (5.45–51); sound is not eternal and there is no sphoṭa (5.57–58).

Virtue is a disposition of buddhi that leads upward but not to release (SK 23, 44); Gauḍapāda defines it through compassion, giving and the Pātañjala restraints and observances. Vedic means are impure through animal killing (SK 2; Vācaspati with Pañcaśikha). The knower of the principles is liberated in any stage of life (verse quoted by Gauḍapāda); outward signs of renunciation without knowledge are a false contentment (Gauḍapāda on SK 50); gifts given with conceit bind (Kramadīpikā); one's own duty supports meditation (SS 3.35).

Bondage is threefold: to prakṛti (absorption from taking the eight prakṛtis as highest), to the modifications (domination by the senses and objects), and through gifts (giving with conceit); release is threefold: by increase of knowledge, by calming of the senses' passion, and by total exhaustion (of virtue and non-virtue), whence isolation (Tattvasamāsa 19–20 with the Kramadīpikā). Strictly, prakṛti is bound and released (SK 62).

Puruṣa witnesses deep sleep and other states (SS 1.148); in concentration (samādhi), deep sleep and liberation puruṣa has the form of Brahman — in the first two with seed, in liberation with the seed destroyed (SS 5.116–117). The SK itself does not analyse waking, dream and sleep.

In the Sāṃkhya Sūtra the practice of the principles proceeds by giving up each with 'not this, not this', whence discrimination (3.76) — the renunciation of identification with each principle, as in the knowledge 'I am not, not mine, not I' (SK 64).
